video.titulo: Everything We Know About Krakatau's Eruption - Will Another Tsunami Strike?
video.descricao:
Sources: https://tinyurl.com/criticalkrakatoa
Support the channel: https://payhip.com/b/GWENV

The Krakatoa tsunami of December 22nd, 2018 killed more than 400 people around Indonesia's Sunda Strait, and no giant eruption warned anyone it was coming.

Anak Krakatau, the island that grew inside the caldera left by the 1883 collapse, dropped its entire southwestern flank into the sea that night. The rock displaced the water, and the waves reached coasts on Java and Sumatra. That same volcano is erupting again now, and the question people keep asking is whether what we are watching is moving it toward another tsunami.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Krakatoa's Missing Side and the 2018 Tsunami
1:41 Anak Krakatau: The Island That Grew Back After 1883
2:41 How a Falling Mountainside Moves the Sea
4:28 The Warning Signs Hidden in the Satellite Data
7:46 Mapping the Collapse: 230-Foot Blocks on the Seabed
10:27 Is the Island Rebuilding the Same Problem?
12:29 What the Research Can and Cannot Tell Us
14:44 Tsunamis Without Earthquakes, and What to Do on a Coast

Before you watched this, would you have expected a volcano to produce a tsunami without a giant earthquake, or even without a giant eruption? 

Subscribe to Critical Latitude for more on earthquakes, faults, volcanoes and tsunamis, and what the planet is actually doing, with the real science behind it.

SOURCES AND DISCLAIMER
The figures in this video come from Walter et al. in Nature Communications (2019) and the GFZ account of that work, Hunt et al. in Nature Communications (2021), Meredew et al. in the Bulletin of Volcanology (2026), NASA's Earth Observatory, Indonesia's B.M.K.G., and the National Weather Service tsunami safety guidance. Every source is linked at the top of this description. 

This video is educational. It is not a prediction of an imminent collapse, tsunami or evacuation, and live instructions for the Sunda Strait coast come from the Indonesian authorities responsible for it.

In the Sunda Strait, there is a particular chain of islands called the Krakatau Archipelago, with the biggest island being Krakatau Island. The island originally had four volcanoes: Krakatau, Perbuatan, Danan, and Rakata.  During the insanely powerful 1883 Krakatau eruption, the whole volcano itself was completely obliterated, along with Perbuatan and Danan, and 70% of the island, Rakata survived, but lost half of it's body.  The magma chamber was emptied. Krakatau was gone, or so that's what people used to believe.  The chamber was refilled without anyone noticing, and a new volcano emerged right above the grave of the old Krakatau, first noticed 40 years later in 1927, and it has kept rapidly growing ever since. We named it "Anak Krakatau" (Child of Krakatau).   Interestingly, there is an ancient anecdote saying that the islands of Java and Sumatra were once one landmass, but were then violently separated by a Krakatau eruption sometime in the 5th century AD. This is not true. The two islands have always been separated for millions of years. They were recently connected during the Ice Age (Sundaland), but that's simply because of the drop in sea level and had nothing to do with volcanic or tectonic activity.

A section of Crocodile's Island is
missing. It's lying at the bottom of the
ocean on the seabed. Before December
22nd, 2018, that rock was part of a
volcano. Then its southwestern side
collapsed into [music] the sea and a
tsunami hit the surrounding coasts. More
than 400 people died. The volcano
erupting there today belongs to that
same system. So yes, Crocatile has
produced a tsunami in the past and it
can do it again. The question is whether
the eruption we're watching now is
moving it towards another tsunami. To
answer that, we need to follow something
the eruption footage can't show us. The
part of the mountain under the water.
Scientists found huge pieces of volcanic
rock on the seabed broken from the side
of the mountain when it collapsed.
Finding that rock helped them work out
what had happened. But the collapse also
changed the underwater slope. So the
island is growing back on ground that
has changed beneath it. I'm Gwen and
this is Critical Latitude. Here we learn
together about the science behind
different natural disasters and talk
about how we know what we can expect and
what we can do to stay safe. But let's
get back to Crocatau. First, we'll work
out how a falling mountainside can move
the sea. Then we'll follow the evidence
scientists recovered after 2018 and
we'll use that evidence to understand
what would make the risk of another
tsunami a concern. The current
observations in this story are from
September 6th, 2026. Some data may be
revised by the time that you watch this.
I'll put corrections in the description
if it's needed. There's a reason people
worry about tsunamis whenever Crocatile
erupts. People who've heard of Crocodile
before have usually heard of 1883 when a
catastrophic eruption destroyed much of
the old island and generated deadly
tsunamis. But the island we're watching
now grew after that disaster. It's
called Anat Crakatau, meaning child of
Crocatau. It sits in Indonesia in the
Sunda Strait, the stretch of sea between
the islands of Java and Sumatra. The
island rises inside a much larger
bull-shaped hollow or what scientists
call a calera left by the old volcano's
collapse. A lot of that caldera is
underwater. When you see a picture of
the smoking cone, you're seeing a small
part of a much larger landscape. A
picture taken from a boat cuts off what
you can see at the water line. The
underwater slope continues below it and
its shape helps determine how well the
mountain side is supported. That's the
part we need to understand to follow
what happened in 2018. So, let's start
this by talking about the ocean and some
fun elementary science.
So,
if we lower a rock into a container of
water,
the water level rises as the stone takes
up space. But if we drop it in, the same
water is going to have to move much
faster.
I'm going to be honest with you, that
splashed way more than I thought it
would.
Okay, that was just a small
demonstration of displacement. Something
enters a space and the water occupying
that space has to move out of the way. A
volcanic landslide is far more
complicated than just a little rock and
a bowl. The rock and landslides can
break apart when it falls. The seabed
can slope off and the water has a ton of
room to spread. To produce a tsunami,
something has to move a large amount of
water and really suddenly. When you see
an eruption, the height of an ash cloud
doesn't tell us how much water has moved
or can move. A huge volcanic eruption
can be dangerous for many reasons,
including the obvious ash and hot
volcanic material. But in a landslide
like this one, huge chunks of rock crash
into the sea and push the water. Once
that happens, waves can travel away from
the volcano toward people who are far
outside its immediate eruptive area.
That explains how a danger starting on
an island can become a coastal disaster.
It also explains why judging every
eruption against 1883 can be misleading.
The deadly tsunami in 2018 happened
without a major eruption on the scale of
1883s. So, the people around the strait
have reason to be worried even during a
smaller eruption. But without large
eruptions happening, were there any
warning signs that part of the mountain
was about to fall? Researchers went back
through measurements taken before that
collapse, looking for changes that might
explain it. Volcanologist Thomas Valter
and an international team brought
together observations from satellites
and instruments on the ground. Their
